title: CLAT UG 2027 · Full-Length Model Paper 004
subtitle: 120-question full-length practice paper · original passages and questions

passages.title: Why a journey is more than a route
passages.text:
Transport planning often begins with a line on a map: a bus route, a railway corridor or a proposed cycle lane. Yet a journey is experienced as a chain of steps. A passenger must reach a stop, understand the service, wait safely, board, make any necessary transfer and travel from the final stop to the actual destination. A route may be efficient in the abstract while remaining difficult for a person who must cross a busy road, climb stairs or wait in an exposed area.

The concept of connectivity therefore extends beyond the number of routes available. A station can be close to a neighbourhood but poorly connected if the walking path is unsafe or inaccessible. A bus may arrive frequently but fail to connect with a train that leaves only a few minutes later. A fare system may require a passenger to buy a separate ticket for each leg, making a journey expensive even where each individual fare appears modest. These barriers are often called first-mile and last-mile problems, although they may arise at any point in the chain.

Designing for a wider range of users requires more than an average travel-time calculation. A parent travelling with a child, a person using a wheelchair, an older passenger and a night-shift worker may experience the same interchange differently. Reliable lifts, clear signs, sheltered waiting areas, safe crossings and predictable connections can determine whether a service is genuinely usable. These features may appear secondary in a large infrastructure budget, but they influence the value of the main investment.

Transport data should reflect the whole journey. Counting vehicles or measuring average speed gives only part of the picture. Authorities can examine door-to-door travel time, missed connections, walking distance, accessibility complaints and the reliability of transfers. Surveys and observation can reveal problems that ticketing systems do not record, such as a passenger choosing a longer route to avoid an unsafe crossing.

A well-designed transport network is not simply a collection of fast lines. It helps people reach opportunities with reasonable effort, cost and uncertainty. Planning improves when officials ask not only where a vehicle travels, but whether different people can complete the journey safely and predictably. The quality of the connection is measured at the passenger's destination, not at the edge of the map.

passages.title: Coastal wetlands as living infrastructure
passages.text:
Coastal wetlands are sometimes described as unused land because they may appear muddy, flooded or difficult to build upon. That description overlooks the functions these ecosystems perform. Mangroves, salt marshes and other wetland habitats can slow waves, hold sediment, store carbon, support fisheries and provide feeding or breeding areas for birds and aquatic species. Their value is not limited to wildlife conservation; they can also contribute to the protection and livelihoods of coastal communities.

The protective effect is not absolute. A wetland's ability to reduce wave energy depends on its width, vegetation, water depth, storm intensity and the shape of the coast. A narrow or degraded strip may offer less protection than a healthy, connected ecosystem. Nor can wetlands prevent every form of flooding, particularly where extreme water levels coincide with heavy rainfall or where settlements have been built below surrounding water levels. Their contribution should be assessed as part of a broader coastal-risk strategy rather than presented as a complete substitute for engineered defences.

Development pressure can damage wetlands gradually. Roads and embankments may interrupt water flow, while land filling can remove habitat and alter sediment movement. Pollution can weaken vegetation and affect the fish or shellfish on which local communities depend. A project that protects one site but shifts erosion or flooding to another may transfer rather than solve the problem. Planning should therefore examine the wider coastal system and the cumulative effects of multiple projects.

Restoration also requires patience. Planting mangrove seedlings is visible and easy to count, but survival depends on tides, soil conditions, freshwater supply and the availability of suitable habitat. Restoring the natural flow of water may be more important than planting more trees in a location where seedlings cannot establish. Monitoring should record survival, biodiversity, shoreline change and benefits to local livelihoods over time.

Wetlands are best understood as living infrastructure. They provide services that may be difficult to reproduce with concrete, but they need space, ecological conditions and long-term stewardship. Their protection can reduce risk and support communities, although it must be combined with responsible land-use planning and preparedness for hazards that ecosystems cannot fully absorb.

passages.title: Archives and the meaning of a public record
passages.text:
An archive is often imagined as a quiet room filled with old documents. In practice, archives are systems for deciding what evidence is preserved, described and made accessible. They may hold government files, personal letters, maps, photographs, recordings and digital records. These materials allow people to reconstruct decisions, examine institutional conduct and understand how communities have changed. The archive is therefore not merely a place where the past is stored; it is part of the infrastructure through which public memory and accountability are maintained.

No archive can preserve everything. Records are created in enormous quantities, and storage, staff time and preservation costs are limited. Archivists must identify which materials have lasting administrative, legal, cultural or research value. This process is called appraisal. A record that appears routine today may become important later if it explains how a policy was implemented or why a public project changed direction. Appraisal therefore requires documented criteria and professional judgement rather than a simple rule that preserves only unusual or famous documents.

Digital records introduce additional challenges. A file may depend on software that becomes obsolete, a database may be altered without a visible paper trail, and a message may lose its context when separated from the conversation in which it was created. Preserving a digital record may require metadata, version history, checksums and documentation of the system that produced it. A copied file is not necessarily a complete record if the relationship among attachments, timestamps and approvals is lost.

Access also involves balancing interests. Public records can support scrutiny, but some files contain personal information, confidential commercial details or material whose release could create a specific risk. Restrictions should be based on clear rules and reviewed when circumstances change. Excessive secrecy weakens accountability; indiscriminate publication can harm people who had a legitimate expectation of protection. A useful archive explains its access conditions and provides a process for review.

The credibility of an archive depends on both preservation and description. A document that survives but cannot be found is difficult to use. A catalogue that misstates the origin of a file can mislead later readers. Good archival practice records where material came from, what processing has been done and what limitations remain. Public institutions strengthen trust when they treat recordkeeping as a continuing responsibility rather than a task to be completed after a controversy begins.

passages.title: The value of corrections in science journalism
passages.text:
Science journalism often reports findings that are provisional, technical or contested. A study may offer a new estimate, a small experiment may suggest a possible mechanism, or researchers may disagree about how strongly the evidence supports a conclusion. Journalists must explain these developments without turning every uncertainty into a dramatic conflict. They must also resist the temptation to present a single study as though it has settled a question that requires years of research.

Accuracy is not achieved only at the moment an article is published. New information may reveal that a number was transcribed incorrectly, a study population was described too broadly or a quotation omitted an important qualification. A newsroom that corrects an error openly can help readers understand the limits of the original report. A newsroom that quietly changes the text without noting the change may preserve the appearance of certainty while making it difficult for readers to know what happened.

Corrections should be proportionate. A spelling error may require a simple amendment, while a mistake that changes the meaning of a health or policy claim should be prominently explained. An editor should identify what was wrong, what has been corrected and whether the conclusion of the report has changed. Corrections are not a sign that accuracy is unimportant; they are one of the mechanisms by which accuracy is maintained over time.

There is a related distinction between correction and disagreement. A reader who dislikes a finding has not necessarily identified an error. A researcher may challenge an interpretation while accepting that the reported data are accurate. A journalist should examine the basis of the challenge, consult relevant expertise and update the story only when the evidence warrants it. Corrections should not become a way to satisfy the loudest critic or to remove a conclusion merely because it is uncomfortable.

Science reporting also benefits from linking claims to accessible sources. Readers should be able to distinguish a peer-reviewed article, a preprint, an institutional press release and an expert's opinion. The status of the evidence should be described accurately. Trust grows when a newsroom makes its reasoning visible, acknowledges what remains unknown and is willing to amend the record when credible new evidence requires it.

passages.title: Digitising India's cultural heritage

sources.title: Ministry of Culture signs MoU with Google Arts & Culture to digitise and share India's cultural heritage
sources.publisher: Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Culture

passages.text:
Cultural heritage is preserved through physical conservation, research, documentation and the transmission of knowledge between generations. Digital tools can widen access to collections that are geographically dispersed or difficult to visit. High-resolution images, searchable catalogues, virtual exhibitions and recorded explanations may allow students and researchers to encounter material beyond the walls of a museum. Yet digitisation does not make the original object unnecessary. Physical conservation, local context and the rights of communities connected to the heritage remain important.

On 5 November 2026, the Ministry of Culture signed a memorandum of understanding with Google Arts & Culture to digitise and share aspects of India's cultural heritage. The Press Information Bureau described the partnership as covering the breadth of India's heritage, including monuments and archaeological sites protected by the Archaeological Survey of India, collections held by national museums, manuscripts being documented under the Gyan Bharatam initiative, and crafts, performing arts and living traditions supported by institutions under the Ministry. The MoU was signed at a virtual ceremony in the presence of officials from the Ministry and Google Arts & Culture.

A memorandum of understanding records an agreed framework for cooperation, but it should not be confused with a completed digital catalogue of every collection named. Each project requires decisions about selection, image quality, metadata, language, permissions and long-term preservation. A photograph may be technically clear but historically misleading if its description omits the object's context. A digital platform may increase visibility while still excluding people who lack reliable connectivity or digital literacy.

Digitisation can also help institutions manage knowledge. Consistent metadata may make it easier to compare objects across collections, identify gaps in documentation and connect related records. But standardisation should not erase local names or different interpretations. A living tradition may have multiple forms, and communities may prefer that particular knowledge not be distributed without consultation. The process should therefore include curators, scholars and the people whose heritage is represented.

The partnership's public value will depend on what is actually documented, whether the material is accessible and whether the records are maintained after the initial project. Digital access can complement conservation and education, but it cannot replace responsibility for the original heritage. The announcement establishes an intention to collaborate; its results must be assessed through completed records, quality of context and sustained public use.

passages.title: Indian Navy's rescue of fishing vessel Azini

sources.title: Indian Navy successfully rescues hijacked fishing vessel Azini off the coast of Somalia
sources.publisher: Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Defence

passages.text:
Piracy in busy maritime corridors threatens crews, shipping operations and the security of trade routes. A vessel that is seized may be used to hold people for ransom or, in some circumstances, as a platform from which further attacks are organised. Responding to such incidents can require surveillance, coordination among military platforms and careful action to protect hostages. The safety of crew members is a central consideration because an operation designed to recover a ship must avoid creating greater danger for the people aboard it.

On 3 November 2026, the Press Information Bureau reported that the Indian Navy had rescued the fishing vessel Azini from armed pirates off the coast of Somalia. The release said that the operation lasted more than 48 hours and resulted in the safe rescue of all 20 crew members, with no casualties or injuries. The vessel had reportedly been hijacked by an armed pirate group earlier in the previous month off the north-eastern coast of Somalia. The release described a concern that the vessel could be used as a 'mother ship' for further attacks on merchant shipping.

The operation involved a mission-deployed naval warship supported by a maritime reconnaissance aircraft. According to the release, the platforms located the vessel through surveillance, tracked its movements and used calibrated non-kinetic measures to contain its movement and prevent escape. Marine Commandos were augmented through a precision airdrop by an Indian Air Force C-17 aircraft. The account describes an operation involving different assets and branches of the armed forces rather than a single ship acting alone.

The incident took place in a region important to Indian Ocean shipping. Maritime security requires more than the ability to respond after a hijacking. It also depends on information-sharing, patrol patterns, cooperation with other states, protection of seafarers and the ability to distinguish a genuine threat from ordinary maritime activity. A successful rescue may deter some criminal activity, but it does not by itself eliminate the conditions that enable piracy.

The release presents the operation as evidence of preparedness and inter-service coordination. Those are official characterisations of the event. A broader assessment of maritime security would require information about incidents over time, regional cooperation and the protection of commercial shipping. The immediate outcome reported was specific: the vessel was secured and all 20 crew members were rescued without injury.

passages.title: Indian Railways freight performance in October 2026

sources.title: Indian Railways registers freight loading of 145.07 million tonnes in October 2026
sources.publisher: Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Railways

passages.text:
Freight transportation is an important part of the logistics system because it connects mines, factories, farms, ports and markets. Railways can move large volumes over long distances, potentially reducing road congestion and supporting industries that require regular deliveries. Freight performance is commonly reported through the weight of goods loaded during a period, but the figure alone does not explain the distance travelled, the type of commodity, the reliability of delivery or the cost to customers.

The Ministry of Railways reported that Indian Railways loaded 145.07 million tonnes of freight during October 2026, compared with 133.93 million tonnes in October 2025. The Press Information Bureau release dated 4 November 2026 described this as an increase of 8.32 per cent and as the highest-ever freight loading for an October month. It also reported cumulative freight loading of 978.78 million tonnes during April to October 2026, surpassing the corresponding period performance of FY 2025–26.

The release highlighted growth in several categories. It reported higher food-grain loading, domestic coal loading, other goods and domestic containers compared with October 2025. It also noted an increase in coal supply to power houses. These details show why commodity composition matters. A rise in total tonnage may reflect increased movement in one or more sectors, while different commodities have different loading requirements, handling arrangements and implications for industrial activity.

Freight loading is an activity measure rather than a complete measure of service quality. A railway may move more tonnes while also facing congestion, longer dwell times or uneven performance across routes. Customers may care about predictability, damage rates, cost and the time required for goods to reach their destination. A fuller assessment would combine loading volumes with service reliability, terminal capacity, wagon availability and the share of goods transferred from road to rail.

The October figure therefore provides a useful snapshot of traffic handled by the network. It should be interpreted alongside the cumulative period and commodity-level information, not as proof by itself that every part of the logistics system has improved. Freight growth can support economic activity, but its lasting value depends on timely delivery, efficient use of infrastructure and the ability to serve a diverse set of customers.

passages.title: International Maize Conference 2026

sources.title: 1st International Maize Conference 2026 calls for higher productivity, innovative breeding and farmer-centric research
sources.publisher: Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Agriculture & Farmers Welfare

passages.text:
Maize is used for food, animal feed, fodder and industrial applications. Its role in agriculture therefore extends beyond the grain consumed directly by households. Demand from livestock, food processing and energy-related uses can influence cropping decisions, prices and the requirements placed on seed systems. A strategy for improving maize productivity must take account of local climate, soil, water availability, farm size and the crops that might otherwise be grown on the same land.

The first International Maize Conference 2026 began in Hyderabad on 2 November 2026 at the JD Convention Centre. The Press Information Bureau described its theme as 'Maize Revolution for Food, Feed, Fodder, Fuel and Sustainability in the Changing World'. The event brought together scientists, policymakers, agricultural institutions and industry stakeholders to discuss research, productivity and value-chain development. The release highlighted high-yielding varieties and hybrids, improved nutritional quality, efficient resource use, mechanisation and stronger seed systems.

Research can raise yields through better genetics, agronomy and crop management, but the transfer of a technology from a research station to a farm is not automatic. Farmers need access to suitable seed, timely advice, credit and markets. A variety developed for one region may perform differently under another region's rainfall or soil conditions. Extension services can help adapt recommendations and collect feedback from cultivators, while field trials can identify unintended effects before a technology is promoted widely.

A systems approach is important because crop choices interact. Expanding maize in one season may affect the availability of land for oilseeds or pulses. Higher output may not improve farm income if market access is weak or input costs rise faster than sale prices. The conference discussion, as reported by PIB, called for research and extension to translate into better farm profitability and livelihoods, not only higher production figures.

Conference themes and statements identify priorities, but they do not establish that productivity has already increased. Outcomes would need to be examined through farm-level yield data, costs, income, resource use and the resilience of production under changing conditions. The event provides a forum for the agricultural research and policy community to consider these connected questions.

passages.title: Recovering cobalt and nickel from industrial residues

sources.title: BARC, HWB and MIDHANI sign tripartite MoU for recovery of cobalt and nickel from plant reverts
sources.publisher: Press Information Bureau, Department of Atomic Energy

passages.text:
Industrial processes can leave behind residues that still contain valuable metals. A material treated as waste in one production system may become a source of inputs if it can be processed safely and economically. Recovering metals from such residues can reduce the need for primary extraction, conserve resources and support a circular economy. However, recovery depends on the composition of the residue, the purity required by the next user, the cost of processing and the management of any hazardous by-products.

On 3 November 2026, the Press Information Bureau reported that the Heavy Water Board (HWB), Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC) and Mishra Dhatu Nigam Limited (MIDHANI) had signed a tripartite memorandum of understanding to collaborate on recovery and production of cobalt and nickel from plant reverts. HWB is a constituent unit of the Department of Atomic Energy, BARC is a research centre under that department and MIDHANI is a Hyderabad-based public sector enterprise under the Ministry of Defence. The MoU was signed on 27 October 2026.

The collaboration is intended to combine different capabilities. HWB contributes technological expertise, BARC contributes scientific and research capacity, and MIDHANI contributes industrial experience. The metals named in the agreement have applications in advanced batteries, electric vehicles, stainless steel, aerospace, defence and high-performance superalloys. Recovery from secondary resources may therefore have both industrial and strategic significance.

An MoU establishes a framework for cooperation; it is not proof that a commercially viable recovery process has already been demonstrated at scale. Research may be needed to improve extraction efficiency, reduce impurities and ensure that the recovered material meets the requirements of industrial users. A process that works in a laboratory may require further testing before it can be integrated into continuous production. Economics also matter: the value of the recovered metal must justify the equipment, energy, labour and environmental controls involved.

The initiative reflects an effort to use domestic research and manufacturing capabilities to recover materials from industrial residues. Its success should be assessed through demonstrated recovery rates, product quality, safety, cost and the volume of material that can be processed reliably. The wider idea is that industrial by-products can become useful inputs where technology and responsible management make recovery feasible.

passages.title: School-led e-waste collection under Special Campaign 6

sources.title: Special Campaign 6 concludes with nationwide e-waste awareness and collection drive
sources.publisher: Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Education

passages.text:
Electronic waste includes discarded phones, computers, batteries, chargers and other electrical or electronic equipment. Such items may contain materials that can be recovered, but they can also include substances that require careful handling. Disposing of e-waste with ordinary household rubbish may expose workers and the environment to avoidable risks. Responsible management involves collection, safe storage, transport to authorised processing channels and public awareness about how to dispose of unwanted devices.

The Ministry of Education's Department of School Education and Literacy observed Special Campaign 6 from 2 to 31 October 2026, with a nationwide focus on administrative efficiency, cleanliness and responsible e-waste management. In a release dated 6 November 2026, the Press Information Bureau reported participation by more than two crore students and teachers across 2.85 lakh schools. It stated that 58.79 lakh e-waste items were collected through the campaign and described the role of school activities and Eco Clubs for Mission LiFE in promoting awareness.

The campaign also included administrative housekeeping measures. The release reported that 41,181 files were reviewed and 31,010 files were weeded out, while 1,84,828 square feet of office space was freed. These figures describe different kinds of activity: e-waste collection relates to environmental management, while file review and disposal relate to the organisation of official records and office space. They should not be combined into a single measure of environmental impact.

Schools can influence behaviour because students take information into households and communities. A collection drive can make the problem visible and create a practical route for handing in old devices. But awareness and collection are only early stages. The environmental benefit depends on what happens after collection: whether items reach authorised processors, whether reusable devices are separated appropriately and whether hazardous components are managed safely. A large collection count is not, by itself, proof of complete recycling.

The campaign's scale indicates broad participation, but long-term success depends on regular collection systems, reliable downstream processing and repeated education. The reported figures are campaign outputs. To measure environmental outcomes, authorities would need to track the final treatment of collected items, recovered materials and the reduction in unsafe disposal.

passages.title: Confidentiality in a mediation process
passages.text:
Assume the following mediation principle. A statement made by a participant solely for the purpose of settling a dispute is confidential and cannot ordinarily be used as evidence in a later adjudication. The principle applies to settlement offers, concessions and communications made in a mediation session. It does not protect a document or fact that existed independently of the mediation, merely because a participant refers to it during the discussion. Exceptions may apply where disclosure is necessary to establish that a settlement was concluded or where a separate legal duty requires disclosure.

The purpose is to allow parties to explore compromise without fearing that every proposed concession will later be treated as an admission of liability. A business may offer a partial payment to avoid the cost of a long dispute even while maintaining that it has a valid defence. If the offer could automatically be used to prove that the business accepted the claim, parties might avoid meaningful negotiation. Confidentiality is therefore intended to encourage candour, not to prevent a court from examining independent evidence.

Suppose a contractor tells a supplier during mediation, 'I could pay half the disputed amount to close the matter this week.' Under the principle, the offer is ordinarily confidential and cannot be used simply to show that the contractor admitted owing the entire amount. But an invoice created before mediation remains an independent document. A participant cannot make the invoice confidential merely by placing it on the mediation table.

The parties may also need to prove that they reached a binding settlement. If a signed settlement agreement is disputed, the communications and documents necessary to determine whether the agreement was concluded may fall within the stated exception. The exception should not become a general licence to publish every negotiation note. Disclosure should be limited to what is genuinely needed for that purpose.

The principle protects the process while recognising that confidentiality is not absolute. A decision-maker should ask why the material was created, whether it existed independently, what purpose disclosure would serve and whether a specific exception applies. The label 'mediation' is not enough by itself; the connection between the material and the settlement process must be examined.

A careful decision should be based on the circumstances available at the time and on reasons that can be explained to the people affected. General labels or assumptions should not replace examination of the actual evidence. This also makes later review more consistent and useful.

passages.title: Mitigation of loss after a breach
passages.text:
Assume a contract principle. When one party breaches an agreement and causes loss, the injured party may recover loss that was reasonably foreseeable and sufficiently connected to the breach. The injured party must take reasonable steps to limit avoidable loss, but is not required to take extraordinary risks, accept an unreasonable substitute or incur disproportionate expense. Loss that could reasonably have been avoided may be reduced when compensation is assessed.

Mitigation does not require the injured party to behave as though the breach were harmless. A buyer whose supplier fails to deliver essential materials may obtain replacement goods from another supplier, even if the replacement costs more. The buyer should act reasonably in the circumstances, considering urgency, availability, quality and the cost of waiting. A buyer need not accept a substitute that is materially inferior or unsafe merely because it is cheaper.

Suppose a hospital orders a specialised component for a medical device and the supplier fails to deliver on time. The hospital purchases a compatible component from another supplier at a higher price after checking that it meets the required safety standard. The additional reasonable cost may be recoverable. If the hospital instead waits several months despite an available compatible replacement and then claims all resulting losses, a decision-maker may examine whether the delay was avoidable.

The principle also limits claims that are too remote. A seller may foresee that late delivery will cause ordinary production disruption, but may not know that the buyer has promised an unusually large penalty to an unrelated third party. If that special consequence was not communicated or reasonably apparent when the contract was made, it may not be recoverable under the stated rule.

Mitigation is a standard of reasonable conduct, not perfection judged with hindsight. The injured party may make a reasonable choice that later turns out to be less successful than expected. A decision-maker should evaluate what was known at the time, what alternatives were available, whether the response was proportionate and whether the claimed loss was connected to the breach.

A careful decision should be based on the circumstances available at the time and on reasons that can be explained to the people affected. General labels or assumptions should not replace examination of the actual evidence. This also makes later review more consistent and useful.

passages.title: A licence condition and proportionality
passages.text:
Assume an administrative principle. A regulator may attach conditions to a licence where the conditions are authorised by the governing rule and reasonably connected to the risk that the licence is intended to control. A condition must not go further than necessary to address that risk when a less restrictive condition would provide comparable protection. The regulator should explain the connection between the activity, the risk and the chosen condition.

A condition may be preventive rather than punitive. A food business may be required to maintain temperature logs because safe storage is central to the activity. A construction permit may require noise limits during specified hours to protect nearby residents. The fact that a condition imposes cost does not make it disproportionate, but the regulator should be able to explain why the requirement is relevant and why its scope is reasonable.

Suppose a small bakery is licensed to sell food and the inspection identifies a risk arising from inadequate refrigeration. The regulator requires calibrated temperature records for the refrigerators and periodic maintenance. Those conditions are directly related to the identified risk. If the regulator instead prohibits the bakery from using its outdoor seating area, without evidence that seating is connected to refrigeration or food safety, the condition may lack the required connection.

The principle also requires consideration of alternatives. If a shorter inspection interval and a targeted repair would address the risk, a complete closure may be excessive unless the danger is immediate and cannot be controlled in a less restrictive way. Conversely, a minor condition may be inadequate where the risk is serious and recurring. Proportionality does not mean choosing the cheapest measure regardless of effectiveness.

A licence holder may challenge a condition by identifying the absence of authority, the weak link between the condition and the risk, or a practical alternative that would provide similar protection. The regulator need not adopt every alternative proposed, but should engage with the evidence and give reasons. The test is whether the condition is authorised, relevant and no broader than reasonably required for the regulatory purpose.

A careful decision should be based on the circumstances available at the time and on reasons that can be explained to the people affected. General labels or assumptions should not replace examination of the actual evidence. This also makes later review more consistent and useful.

passages.title: Ownership of a commissioned creative work
passages.text:
Assume an intellectual-property principle for this problem. When a client commissions a creator to produce an original work, payment for the work does not automatically transfer every right in it. Ownership and permitted use depend on the agreement between the parties. If the agreement expressly transfers copyright, the transfer applies to the rights and scope stated. If it grants a licence, the creator retains ownership while the client may use the work within the licence's limits.

A licence may be limited by purpose, duration, territory, platform or type of use. A designer may allow a company to use a logo on packaging and websites but not to sell the artwork as a standalone product. A photographer may grant a one-year licence for a campaign while retaining the right to use the photograph in a portfolio, subject to any confidentiality term. The scope should be interpreted from the wording and context of the agreement rather than assumed from the fact that the client paid the invoice.

Suppose a restaurant pays an illustrator to create a menu image. The contract says the restaurant may use the image on printed menus and its own website for three years. The restaurant later wants to put the image on merchandise sold to the public. That use may fall outside the stated licence, even though the restaurant paid the agreed fee. It should obtain an additional licence or a transfer that covers the new purpose.

The principle also recognises that a creator cannot ignore a valid transfer simply because the work is personally meaningful. If the contract clearly transfers specified rights, the creator must respect that agreement. But a transfer of one right does not necessarily transfer all rights, and an agreement should be read for the precise rights, media and period it covers.

The practical lesson is to define ownership and use before work begins. Parties should identify whether the arrangement is an assignment or a licence, list the intended uses and state whether new uses require additional permission. Payment, delivery and ownership are related but distinct questions. A clear agreement reduces disputes when a project expands beyond its original purpose.

A careful decision should be based on the circumstances available at the time and on reasons that can be explained to the people affected. General labels or assumptions should not replace examination of the actual evidence. This also makes later review more consistent and useful.

passages.title: Refunds for a cancelled service
passages.text:
Assume a consumer-contract principle. Where a trader cancels a service and the consumer has paid in advance, the trader must refund the amount attributable to the service not provided, unless the consumer has agreed to a lawful alternative remedy. A trader may deduct a reasonable amount for a distinct service already delivered if the contract clearly identifies it and the consumer received a real benefit. A vague administrative charge cannot be imposed merely because the trader prefers not to return the money.

The principle distinguishes cancellation by the trader from a consumer's voluntary cancellation. If a concert organiser cancels an event entirely, the consumer has not received the promised event. If a customer chooses not to attend a concert that takes place as scheduled, different contractual terms may apply. A trader should not treat these situations as identical. The reason for cancellation and the portion of the service already delivered matter.

Suppose a training provider sells a ten-session course and cancels the final four sessions because the venue becomes unavailable. The consumer has attended six sessions. If the contract permits a refund for sessions not provided, the provider should return the attributable amount. It may not retain the entire fee by claiming that registration and administration costs were incurred, unless those charges are separately agreed and genuinely relate to a benefit already delivered.

If the provider offers a replacement course at a different location and time, it should give the consumer a real choice where the contract or applicable rule requires it. An alternative that is unusable for the consumer may not be an effective substitute. A credit note may be convenient, but should not automatically replace a cash refund where the consumer is entitled to repayment.

The principle aims to prevent a trader from retaining payment for a service that was not supplied. It does not require a refund for every dissatisfaction or for a service properly delivered. The decision-maker should identify the party who cancelled, the service actually provided, the contract terms and the value of any genuine partial benefit.

A careful decision should be based on the circumstances available at the time and on reasons that can be explained to the people affected. General labels or assumptions should not replace examination of the actual evidence. This also makes later review more consistent and useful.

passages.title: Use of a deposit in a booking agreement
passages.text:
Assume a booking principle. A deposit may be retained after cancellation only to the extent permitted by the agreement and only where the amount is a reasonable estimate of loss or a reasonable charge for a clearly identified reservation service. A term that allows a trader to keep the entire deposit in every circumstance, regardless of the timing of cancellation or the loss actually likely to occur, may be unfair under this principle. The trader must explain the basis for retaining the amount.

A deposit can serve a legitimate function. A hotel may reserve a room that it could otherwise offer to another guest, and a venue may incur costs when a booking is made. The closer a cancellation occurs to the reserved date, the harder it may be to resell the capacity. But the amount retained should reflect the relevant circumstances rather than operate as an automatic penalty unrelated to loss.

Suppose a customer books a hall six months in advance and pays a deposit. The customer cancels two months later, leaving four months for the venue to find another booking. If the venue resells the same date at the same price, retaining the entire deposit may not be reasonable unless the agreement identifies a separate service or cost that justifies it. If the customer cancels the day before the event and the venue cannot rebook, some retention may be justified under the agreement.

The trader should also distinguish costs already incurred from hypothetical costs. A non-refundable supplier payment may be relevant if it was necessary for the booking and the customer was informed of it. A general claim that 'administration takes time' is not enough by itself to justify a large deduction. The customer may challenge the calculation and ask for the relevant basis.

The principle balances the trader's legitimate reliance on a reservation with the customer's right not to lose money arbitrarily. It asks whether the term was clear, whether the retained amount is connected to a real service or reasonable loss and whether the cancellation circumstances have been considered.

passages.title: Does a school meal programme improve attendance?
passages.text:
A district education office proposes expanding a school meal programme. Its report points to a school where attendance rose from 82 per cent to 89 per cent after meals were introduced. The report argues that meals encourage children to attend and that the programme should therefore be extended to every school in the district. A parent group supports better nutrition but asks whether the school also received new teachers and transport support during the same period.

The education office replies that the meal programme is the most visible change and that teachers reported fewer students leaving school before lunch. A researcher notes that attendance can change for several reasons, including seasonal work, weather, illness, examination schedules and the quality of teaching. A single school's before-and-after result cannot isolate the effect of meals if other conditions changed at the same time.

The researcher proposes comparing schools that introduce the programme at different dates. The evaluation would record attendance, punctuality, meal uptake, student health indicators and any changes in staffing or transport. It would also examine whether the effect differs by age group or household income. A meal programme might improve attendance for younger children while having little effect on older students who face other barriers.

The parent group adds that a programme should be assessed for nutritional quality and reliability. If meals are irregular or unsuitable for dietary needs, the intended benefit may not arise. The office agrees to publish menus, monitor food safety and create a mechanism for reporting missed deliveries. It argues that the possibility of imperfect evaluation should not prevent a beneficial service from expanding, but accepts that the scale and design can be adjusted in response to evidence.

The question is not whether a rise from 82 to 89 per cent is encouraging; it is. The question is whether that increase can be attributed to meals and whether it is likely to occur elsewhere. A careful evaluation can distinguish association from causation while also checking that the service is delivered safely and consistently.

A careful decision should be based on the circumstances available at the time and on reasons that can be explained to the people affected. General labels or assumptions should not replace examination of the actual evidence. This also makes later review more consistent and useful.

passages.title: Multilingual access in a public library
passages.text:
A city library system is considering adding multilingual signs and service guides. The director argues that clearer signs will help residents who are more comfortable in languages other than the dominant language. The finance committee worries that printing and updating many versions will be expensive and that translations may become outdated when services change. A community group says that the current signs are confusing even for fluent speakers because they use technical terms and inconsistent symbols.

The library tests new signs in two branches. Visitors are asked to find the children's section, computer room and accessible entrance. The average time to locate these areas falls after the signs are installed. The director concludes that multilingual signage improves access. A researcher points out that the trial also replaced small text with larger lettering and added symbols, so the improvement may not be caused by translation alone.

The researcher proposes a second test with four versions: the existing signs, simplified dominant-language signs, signs with symbols and multilingual signs. Visitors would be asked to complete the same tasks, with the order of tasks varied to reduce learning effects. The library would also consult speakers of each language to check that the wording is natural and that a translation does not create a misleading impression.

The community group argues that printed signs are only one part of access. Staff should know how to direct visitors, online pages should offer the same information and the library should avoid asking visitors to disclose unnecessary personal details to request help. The finance committee suggests updating the most important signs first and using a standard template so that later service changes can be made consistently.

The evidence from the first trial supports the usefulness of the new sign package but does not isolate the effect of multilingual wording. A more careful test can identify which changes matter most. The library should also consider whether the signs improve independent access for visitors who need them, not only whether the average visitor completes a task faster.

A careful decision should be based on the circumstances available at the time and on reasons that can be explained to the people affected. General labels or assumptions should not replace examination of the actual evidence. This also makes later review more consistent and useful.

passages.title: Urban tree planting and survival rates
passages.text:
A municipal corporation announces that it has planted 50,000 saplings along roads and in public parks. The mayor describes the programme as a major step towards reducing urban heat. An environmental group welcomes the effort but asks how many saplings are likely to survive. It argues that a planting target is an input measure and that shade will depend on the trees reaching maturity, being suited to the local climate and receiving water and maintenance.

The corporation replies that survival cannot be known immediately and that planting a large number is necessary to create a future canopy. It also says that residents have been invited to adopt trees and that contractors are responsible for watering during the first year. A councillor asks whether the adopted trees are distributed evenly across neighbourhoods or concentrated in areas with more organised resident groups.

An independent evaluator proposes marking a sample of saplings and recording survival at six, twelve and twenty-four months. The sample should cover different species, soil conditions and neighbourhoods. The evaluator also recommends measuring shade coverage and surface temperature rather than assuming that every surviving tree provides the same cooling benefit. Mature trees, young trees and trees planted in narrow roadside pits may have different effects.

The environmental group argues that dead saplings should be replaced only after the cause of failure is understood. Replanting without correcting water shortages, soil compaction or poor species selection may reproduce the same loss. The corporation accepts that maintenance and site selection need attention, but says that tree planting should be integrated with footpaths, utilities and street safety rather than treated as a standalone activity.

The dispute concerns how progress is measured. The number planted is useful for monitoring activity, but it does not establish the amount of shade or heat reduction delivered. The evaluation should combine survival, location, species, canopy development and maintenance. A credible programme reports both the scale of planting and the condition of the trees over time.

A careful decision should be based on the circumstances available at the time and on reasons that can be explained to the people affected. General labels or assumptions should not replace examination of the actual evidence. This also makes later review more consistent and useful.

passages.title: A delivery window for local businesses
passages.text:
A city is testing a delivery-window system in a busy market district. Under the proposal, larger delivery vehicles may enter during two morning windows, while smaller electric vehicles and handcarts may deliver throughout the day. The transport department argues that the system will reduce congestion during shopping hours without preventing businesses from receiving supplies. Shop owners say that their deliveries arrive at different times and that fixed windows may increase storage costs or cause goods to arrive after they are needed.

The department cites a pilot street where average vehicle speed increased after restrictions were introduced. A market association says that the pilot was conducted during a period when roadworks had ended and school holidays had begun. It also argues that speed alone does not measure whether deliveries are reliable or whether businesses lose sales because supplies arrive late.

A logistics researcher proposes collecting data on traffic volume, loading time, delivery punctuality, business stockouts and pedestrian safety. The study should compare similar streets and include interviews with small businesses that cannot afford large storage spaces. It should also record whether delivery companies shift to smaller vehicles or simply move their activity to nearby roads, transferring congestion rather than reducing it.

The department suggests a flexible booking system in which businesses can reserve a delivery slot. The market association supports a trial but wants exceptions for perishable goods and emergency replenishment. The department responds that exceptions should be defined clearly so they do not become a way to avoid the scheme entirely. Both sides agree that enforcement should be consistent and that the trial should have a public review date.

The proposal has several possible outcomes: fewer large vehicles at peak hours, longer delivery journeys, changes in inventory practices and effects on pedestrian safety. A rise in average speed may be encouraging, but it cannot settle whether the policy is fair or efficient. The city needs evidence about the entire delivery chain and the different constraints faced by businesses of different sizes.

A careful decision should be based on the circumstances available at the time and on reasons that can be explained to the people affected. General labels or assumptions should not replace examination of the actual evidence. This also makes later review more consistent and useful.
